sweep_summary: Five title hits for Romanian. Two are about word stress: Roca 1999 (Eurotyp chapter; paywalled at De Gruyter, WAF-blocked; the catalog already carries its StressTyp2 excerpt 1717) and Iscrulescu 2006 (Benjamins, closed; abstract obtained via OpenAlex and saved). The Iscrulescu abstract explicitly argues that Romanian nominal stress is weight-insensitive (syllabic trochees, final-consonant final stress as opacity), contra Steriade 1984's weight-sensitive analysis, so it contradicts the mechanism behind the catalog's 'weight-hedged' coding at the analysis level; the full paper is high priority. Ulivi 1985 (secondary stress in Daco-Romanian dialects, RRL) is print-only (lingv.ro archive starts 2006) and concerns secondary stress. Göbbel 2003 and Swerts 2007 are sentence-level prosody (focus/pitch accent), not word stress; Swerts's TLDR ('accent distribution.. demarcative rather than contrastive' in Romanian) was recorded. Iscrulescu's ROA 887 dissertation was downloaded and checked: no stress-placement statement. No new first-hand statement supersedes Steriade 1984. DuckDuckGo/Bing/Google/HathiTrust/Internet Archive were unreachable or could not be reached by automated download, so discovery relied on Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, ROA and publisher/journal sites.

new_statements.quote: The acoustic properties of two types of prosodic prominence, stress and focus at the lexical and sentence levels, respectively, are examined in Romanian. Real three-syllable words were produced by 9 native speakers in two sentential contexts [...]. The position of stress was systematically varied, so it appeared on each of the three syllable positions. Analyses of over 3,500 vowels show that duration and F0 are robust correlates of lexical stress in Romanian, consistent with cross-linguistic patterns.
new_statements.citation: Spinu, Laura. 2026. The acoustic manifestation of stress and focus in Romanian. Probus 38(1): 7-32.
new_statements.locator: Abstract (as served by OpenAlex/Crossref metadata for doi:10.1515/probus-2026-0001); full text (pp. 7-32) not obtained
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (abstract_inverted_index reassembled) and jats abstract): the quoted sentences are there word for word; the '[..]' drops only the parenthetical on the two focus contexts.bin). Reading: the abstract states that stress in real trisyllabic words was placed on each of the three syllable positions and that duration and F0 cue 'lexical stress'; it states no placement rule. Note that 'lexical' there contrasts with sentence-level focus (word-level stress), not 'lexically specified', so the lexical (unpredictable) label rests on the three-position fact together with the catalog's WALS 14A 'No fixed stress', which is a fair use of the fixed list. 'Refines' is right: compatible with WALS 14A/15…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's WALS-based 'lexical stress' / 'no fixed stress' entry and with the StressTyp2 U/P (final-if-heavy, else penult) rule only as a lexical system; it adds that antepenultimate stress occurs in real trisyllabic words (beyond WALS 15A 'ultimate or penultimate') and that duration and F0 are the acoustic cues, focus enhancing them additively. Not a placement source; the catalog rule field for this record is empty.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The abstract treats Romanian stress as lexical (word-level) stress whose position is not fixed: in real trisyllabic words it can sit on the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable, and its acoustic correlates are duration and F0 (with slightly more peripheral vowels). No placement rule is stated in the abstract; the full text (CC-BY, but behind the degruyterbrill.com WAF: automated download 202/empty twice, direct download 405, no archived copy at the Internet Archive, no repository copy) could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: All three works concern standard (Daco-)Romanian; Klein 2007 also treats Siswati (ssw), a Bantu language, in its second half, with no tone or stress statement for it.

new_statements.quote: Real three-syllable words were produced by 9 native speakers in two sentential contexts: with focus on the target word (focus context) and with focus on a word later in the sentence (non-focus context). The position of stress was systematically varied, so it appeared on each of the three syllable positions. Analyses of over 3,500 vowels show that duration and F0 are robust correlates of lexical stress in Romanian, consistent with cross-linguistic patterns.

The abstract continues: 'Focus further enhances these stress-related…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (Steriade 1984: stress confined to the last three syllables, penult vs antepenult partly rule-governed, partly lexical; final stress rare and suffix-bound) and identical in content to the existing Spinu 2026 statement held by the project (same abstract): it confirms that all three positions of the three-syllable window occur in real words and adds the acoustic correlates (duration, F0); it gives no weight condition or default, so it neither supports nor contradicts the 'weight-hedged' kind. No new text beyond what the first reader had.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Romanian word stress is treated as lexical: in real trisyllabic words stress can fall on the antepenult, the penult or the final syllable (all three positions are attested and were used as stimuli); stressed vowels are longer and higher in F0, and sentence focus enhances these cues additively. The abstract states no placement rule or default.
new_statements.identity_note: Standard (Daco-)Romanian; 9 native speakers, laboratory production study of real trisyllabic words (per abstract); no dialect specified in the metadata.

sources.quote: p.208: 'Stress in Romanian falls on the rightmost syllable of the prosodic word. The prosodic word includes the root and derivational material, excluding inflections and desinence vowels. Thus, the penult is stressed when the final syllable contains the desinence vowel (4a), and the final syllable is stressed in the absence of a desinence vowel (4b).' p.209: 'Romanian also contains a lexically marked stress pattern, with penultimate stress' (kámer-ă, bívol). p.228: 'There is evidence, however, that the stress system of Romanian is not weight sensitive (Chitoran 1996, 1997, 2001).'

sources.quote: I show that nominal stress is best analyzed as weight-insensitive footing (syllabic trochees), contra claims that the system is weight-sensitive (moraic trochees, Steriade 1984). Forms with superficial final vowels are shown to conform to the syllabic trochee pattern (modulo certain items with lexical specification). The necessity of final vowel extrametricality, claimed in previous analyses of Romance stress, is obviated. Stress on the final syllable in words ending in consonants is claimed to represent an instance of phonological opacity
